slides.title: Every "we'll do it later" is a loan
slides.subtitle: Nobody is tracking the balance

slides.lie: We'll document the API later
slides.reality: The types ARE the documentation. Define them first.

slides.lie: I'll check the browser manually later
slides.reality: DevTools MCP lets the agent verify now, in the same session, automatically.

slides.lie: We'll add CI later
slides.reality: Projects without CI accumulate broken states. Set it up on day one.

slides.lie: We'll clean it up later
slides.reality: Later never comes. The review is the quality gate — use it. Require cleanup before merge, not after.

slides.lie: I'll fix it in the next commit
slides.reality: Fix it now. The next commit will introduce new bugs on top of this one.

slides.lie: We'll deprecate it after we finish the new system
slides.reality: Deprecation planning starts at design time. By the time the new system is done, you'll have new priorities. Plan now.

slides.lie: We'll write docs when the API stabilizes
slides.reality: APIs stabilize faster when you document them. The doc is the first test of the design.

slides.lie: We'll make it responsive later
slides.reality: Retrofitting responsive design is 3x harder than building it from the start.

slides.lie: I'll squash it all later
slides.reality: Squashing destroys the development narrative. Prefer clean incremental commits from the start.

slides.lie: I'll split this change later
slides.reality: Large changes are harder to review, riskier to deploy, and harder to revert. Split before submitting, not after.

slides.lie: We'll write the changelog at release time
slides.reality: By then the impact is reconstructed from memory and half of it is missing. Write the entry with the change.

slides.lie: I'll add the feature flag later
slides.reality: If the feature isn't complete, it shouldn't be user-visible. Add the flag now.

slides.lie: I'll add logging after it works
slides.reality: "After" becomes "after the first incident", which is the most expensive moment to discover you're blind. Instrument as you build.

slides.lie: Alert on everything important, we'll tune later
slides.reality: A noisy pager trains people to ignore it. The tuning never happens; the missed real page does.

slides.lie: We'll optimize later
slides.reality: Performance debt compounds. Fix obvious anti-patterns now, defer micro-optimizations.

slides.lie: We'll add security later
slides.reality: Security retrofitting is 10x harder than building it in. Add it now.

slides.lie: We'll add monitoring later
slides.reality: Add it before launch. You can't debug what you can't see.

slides.lie: I'll write the spec after I code it
slides.reality: That's documentation, not specification. The spec's value is in forcing clarity *before* code.

slides.title: "That's overhead" — is it though?
slides.subtitle: Sometimes yes. Usually not for the reason given.

slides.lie: Performance profiling is overkill
slides.reality: A 1-second performance trace catches issues that hours of code review miss.

slides.lie: CI is too slow
slides.reality: Optimize the pipeline (see CI Optimization below), don't skip it. A 5-minute pipeline prevents hours of debugging.

slides.lie: The migration is too expensive
slides.reality: Compare migration cost to ongoing maintenance cost over 2-3 years. Migration is usually cheaper long-term.

slides.lie: ADRs are overhead
slides.reality: A 10-minute ADR prevents a 2-hour debate about the same decision six months later.

slides.lie: Spawning a reviewer is expensive
slides.reality: Debugging a wrong commit in production is more expensive. The check is bounded; the bug isn't.

slides.lie: Accessibility is a nice-to-have
slides.reality: It's a legal requirement in many jurisdictions and an engineering quality standard.

slides.title: "That's overhead" — is it though?
slides.subtitle: Sometimes yes. Usually not for the reason given.

slides.lie: Branches add overhead
slides.reality: Short-lived branches are free and prevent conflicting work from colliding. Long-lived branches are the problem — merge within 1-3 days.

slides.lie: Asking too many questions wastes their time
slides.reality: Time wasted by 4–6 targeted questions is small. Time wasted by building the wrong thing is enormous, and the user is the one bearing that cost.

slides.lie: Tracing is overkill for our two services
slides.reality: Two services already means cross-service latency questions logs can't answer. Auto-instrumentation makes the cost trivial.

slides.lie: Planning is overhead
slides.reality: Planning is the task. Implementation without a plan is just typing.

slides.lie: Threat modeling is overkill here
slides.reality: Five minutes of "how would I attack this?" prevents the design flaws no control can patch later.

slides.lie: Monitoring is overhead
slides.reality: Not having monitoring means you discover problems from user complaints instead of dashboards.

slides.title: "That's overhead" — is it though?
slides.subtitle: Sometimes yes. Usually not for the reason given.

slides.lie: Fetching docs wastes tokens
slides.reality: Hallucinating an API wastes more. The user debugs for an hour, then discovers the function signature changed. One fetch prevents hours of rework.

slides.lie: The spec will slow us down
slides.reality: A 15-minute spec prevents hours of rework. Waterfall in 15 minutes beats debugging in 15 hours.

slides.lie: It's one big feature; splitting it is overhead
slides.reality: If acceptance criteria cluster into independently testable groups, a monolithic spec forces every downstream task to reason over the whole contract. A ten-line capability map is the cheap alternative.

slides.lie: Tests slow me down
slides.reality: Tests slow you down now. They speed you up every time you change the code later.

slides.title: "It's too small to matter"
slides.subtitle: The threshold nobody defined

slides.lie: This change is trivial, skip CI
slides.reality: Trivial changes break builds. CI is fast for trivial changes anyway.

slides.lie: It's only a small addition to this file
slides.reality: Small diffs still push files past a healthy size and bolt branches onto unrelated flows. Judge the resulting structure, not the diff size.

slides.lie: It's just a version bump
slides.reality: A bump is a behavior change you didn't write. Read the changelog; semver doesn't guarantee no breakage.

slides.lie: Just rename the column, it's one line
slides.reality: During the rollout, old and new code run together — one will query a column that no longer exists. Expand/contract, never rename in place.

slides.lie: This is just a prototype
slides.reality: Prototypes become production code. Build the foundation right.

slides.lie: It's just a small fix, bump the patch
slides.reality: Check what consumers can observe. A behavior change they relied on is a major, whatever the diff size.

slides.title: The excuses that are completely true
slides.subtitle: And still wrong. That's what makes them hard to argue with.

slides.lie: Accepting the Idempotency-Key header is enough
slides.reality: The header is the contract; storing the key against the result is the implementation. A key you accept but don't honour tells the client retrying is safe when it isn't.

slides.lie: Our queue guarantees exactly-once delivery
slides.reality: No queue does across a consumer crash — the broker's ack and your side effect are not in one transaction. Design for at-least-once with idempotent processing.

slides.lie: The DOM must be correct if the tests pass
slides.reality: Unit tests don't test CSS, layout, or real browser rendering. DevTools does.

slides.lie: Manual testing is enough
slides.reality: Manual testing doesn't scale and isn't repeatable. Automate what you can.

slides.lie: It works, that's good enough
slides.reality: Working code that's unreadable, insecure, or architecturally wrong creates debt that compounds.

slides.lie: The tests pass, so it's good
slides.reality: Tests are necessary but not sufficient. They don't catch architecture problems, security issues, or readability concerns.

slides.title: The excuses that are completely true
slides.subtitle: And still wrong. That's what makes them hard to argue with.

slides.lie: The types make it self-documenting
slides.reality: Types document structure, not intent. A well-named function explains *why* better than a type signature explains *what*.

slides.lie: It works on my machine
slides.reality: Environments differ. Check CI, check config, check dependencies.

slides.lie: The code is self-documenting
slides.reality: Code shows what. It doesn't show why, what alternatives were rejected, or what constraints apply.

slides.lie: I'll add logging after it works
slides.reality: "After" becomes "after the first incident", which is the most expensive moment to discover you're blind. Instrument as you build.

slides.lie: It's fast on my machine
slides.reality: Your machine isn't the user's. Profile on representative hardware and networks.

slides.lie: The audit passed, so the dependency is safe
slides.reality: Audits match known advisories. They do not detect a newly malicious package or make unreviewed install scripts safe to execute.

slides.title: "I already know"
slides.subtitle: Confidence is not a verification method

slides.lie: It looks right in my mental model
slides.reality: Runtime behavior regularly differs from what code suggests. Verify with actual browser state.

slides.lie: I wrote it, so I know it's correct
slides.reality: Authors are blind to their own assumptions. Every change benefits from another set of eyes.

slides.lie: The original author must have had a reason
slides.reality: Maybe. Check git blame — apply Chesterton's Fence. But accumulated complexity often has no reason; it's just the residue of iteration under pressure.

slides.lie: I know what the bug is, I'll just fix it
slides.reality: You might be right 70% of the time. The other 30% costs hours. Reproduce first.

slides.lie: I'm confident, skip the doubt step
slides.reality: Confidence correlates poorly with correctness on novel problems. Moments of certainty are exactly when blind spots hide.

slides.lie: The ask is clear enough
slides.reality: If you can't write the user's desired outcome in one sentence right now, the ask isn't clear. Run Step 1 before deciding.

slides.title: "I already know"
slides.subtitle: Confidence is not a verification method

slides.lie: We've talked enough, I get it
slides.reality: Test it: can you predict their reaction to the next three questions? If not, you don't get it yet.

slides.lie: The user said yes, we're done
slides.reality: If the yes followed a vague restate or an open-ended "sounds good," the yes is hollow. Restate concretely and re-confirm.

slides.lie: The improvement is obvious, no need to re-measure
slides.reality: Then re-measuring is cheap and proves it. Unmeasured wins are how neutral complexity lands.

slides.lie: I can hold it all in my head
slides.reality: Context windows are finite. Written plans survive session boundaries and compaction.

slides.lie: I'm confident about this API
slides.reality: Confidence is not evidence. Training data contains outdated patterns that look correct but break against current versions. Verify.

slides.lie: This is a simple task, no need to check
slides.reality: Simple tasks with wrong patterns become templates. The user copies your deprecated form handler into ten components before discovering the modern approach exists.

slides.title: "Someone else handles that"
slides.subtitle: The framework does not, in fact, handle it

slides.lie: Nobody uses that undocumented behavior
slides.reality: Hyrum's Law: if it's observable, somebody depends on it. Treat every public behavior as a commitment.

slides.lie: The agent should figure out the conventions
slides.reality: It can't read your mind. Write a rules file — 10 minutes that saves hours.

slides.lie: Users will migrate on their own
slides.reality: They won't. Provide tooling, documentation, and incentives — or do the migration yourself (the Churn Rule).

slides.lie: Nobody reads docs
slides.reality: Agents do. Future engineers do. Your 3-months-later self does.

slides.lie: The framework handles performance
slides.reality: Frameworks prevent some issues but can't fix N+1 queries or oversized bundles.

slides.lie: No one would try to exploit this
slides.reality: Automated scanners will find it. Security by obscurity is not security.
